Reared
REERD
v. (past t. and past part.)
From rear, Saxon raeran, to raise. Webster 1828: raised; lifted up; erected; brought up or educated. Scripture uses it of the tabernacle set up, of altars to Baal, and of a monument a man raised to his own name.

Biblical Definition

Reared means raised or set up, and Scripture applies it to three very different erections. It is used of the tabernacle, assembled exactly as God commanded on the first day of the second year: And Moses reared up the tabernacle, and fastened his sockets, and set up the boards thereof, and put in the bars thereof, and reared up his pillars (Exodus 40:18). It is used of the altars of apostasy: he reared up an altar for Baal in the house of Baal, which he had built in Samaria (1 Kings 16:32) of Ahab, and of Manasseh, he built up again the high places which Hezekiah his father had destroyed; and he reared up altars for Baal, and made a grove, as did Ahab king of Israel; and worshipped all the host of heaven (2 Kings 21:3) — a son deliberately undoing his father’s reformation. And it is used of a monument to a man’s own name: Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and reared up for himself a pillar, which is in the king’s dale: for he said, I have no son to keep my name in remembrance; and he called the pillar after his own name (2 Samuel 18:18) — erected by a man who had three sons, and who died in a tree.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines REARED as raised; lifted up; set upright; erected, as a building or a pillar; and, of children and animals, brought up, nursed, or educated.

expand to see more

REARED, pp. — Raised; lifted up; set upright; erected.

Brought up; educated; nursed and trained, as a child or an animal.

REAR, v.t. — To raise; to lift up; to set upright; to erect, as a building or a monument.

To bring to maturity; to breed and nourish; as, to rear cattle or to rear a family.

From Saxon raeran, to raise — a causative form of rise.

Key Scripture

Exodus 40:18 — "And Moses reared up the tabernacle, and fastened his sockets, and set up the boards thereof, and put in the bars thereof, and reared up his pillars."

1 Kings 16:32 — "And he reared up an altar for Baal in the house of Baal, which he had built in Samaria."

2 Kings 21:3 — "For he built up again the high places which Hezekiah his father had destroyed; and he reared up altars for Baal, and made a grove, as did Ahab king of Israel; and worshipped all the host of heaven, and served them."

2 Samuel 18:18 — "Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and reared up for himself a pillar, which is in the king's dale: for he said, I have no son to keep my name in remembrance: and he called the pillar after his own name: and it is called unto this day, Absalom's place."

Modern Corruption

2 Kings 21:3 records a son systematically rebuilding what his father had torn down, which is the standing warning that a reformation is never more than one generation from being reversed.

expand to see more

Hezekiah had removed the high places, broken the images, cut down the groves, and destroyed the brasen serpent Moses had made when Israel began burning incense to it. Manasseh, his son, built up again the high places which Hezekiah his father had destroyed, reared altars for Baal, made a grove, worshipped the host of heaven, set a carved image in the house of the LORD, and made his son pass through the fire. The chapter says he made Judah do worse than the nations God had destroyed before them. No reformation is self-perpetuating. The Reformers understood this and built catechisms, household instruction, and confessions precisely because the recovery of the gospel in one generation guarantees nothing about the next. Deuteronomy 6 puts the duty in the home, at every hour of the day, and Judges 2:10 records what happens when it lapses: there arose another generation after them, which knew not the LORD.

Absalom’s pillar is the smaller and sadder text. He reared it for himself, in the king’s dale, because I have no son to keep my name in remembrance — and 2 Samuel 14:27 says he had three sons and a daughter. Whether they had died or whether he simply judged them insufficient, the monument was self-commissioned and self-named, and the man who built it was buried under a heap of stones in a wood. The contrast with Exodus 40:18 is the whole lesson of the entry: Moses reared up a structure whose pattern he had been given and whose glory he did not claim, and the cloud covered it and the glory of the LORD filled it. What a man rears to his own name is a pillar; what he rears at God’s command is filled.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qum (H6965), to arise, to raise up; natsab (H5324), to set up, to station; banah (H1129), to build; Greek egeiro (G1453), to raise up.

expand to see more

Hebrew qum (H6965) — to arise, to stand, and causatively to raise up; Moses reared up the tabernacle (Exodus 40:18).

Hebrew natsab (H5324) — to station, to set up; reared up for himself a pillar (2 Samuel 18:18).

Hebrew banah (H1129) — to build; the companion verb in 1 Kings 16:32 and 2 Kings 21:3.

Hebrew matstsebah (H4676) — a standing pillar; used both of Jacob’s memorial at Bethel and of pagan sacred stones.

Greek egeiro (G1453) — to raise up; in three days I will raise it up (John 2:19).

Usage

"Moses reared up the tabernacle (Exodus 40:18) — built to a given pattern, and filled with glory."

"He reared up altars for Baal (2 Kings 21:3) — a son undoing his father’s reformation, item by item."

"Absalom… reared up for himself a pillar (2 Samuel 18:18) — self-commissioned, self-named, and buried under stones."
